snippet.title: 7 Days Surviving the Black Death in Medieval London | 1348 Full Documentary
snippet.description:
7 Days Surviving the Black Death in Medieval London — the complete series in one full-length documentary.

In the autumn of 1348, the Black Death arrived in London. Within months it would kill between a third and a half of everyone in the city. This is the story of that catastrophe — not told through kings, battles, or cathedrals, but through seven ordinary people living one day at a time as the plague closed in around them.

Over roughly an hour and a half, you'll spend a full week inside medieval London in 1348: walking the cobbled streets of Cheapside, standing in the cold choir stalls of Westminster Abbey, sitting in a physician's candlelit workroom, and watching the long burial trenches grow at East Smithfield. This is immersive, historically grounded living-history — a reconstruction of what daily life, work, faith, medicine, and death actually looked like for medieval Londoners during the worst pandemic in European history.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📜 WHAT YOU'LL SEE — THE FULL WEEK
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Day 1 — The Apprentice: a young weaver on Cheapside, watching the first death-carts roll past his master's workshop.
Day 2 —  The Monk
Day 3 — The Silk Woman: a craftswoman of Soper Lane fighting to keep her workshop and her trade alive as her workers fall ill.
Day 4 — The Gravedigger: a man at the East Smithfield burial ground who has stopped counting how many he has laid in the rows.
Day 5 — The Alderman: a ward official who keeps showing up to a half-empty Guildhall, quietly bending the rules to protect the living.
Day 6 — The Physician: a Montpellier-trained doctor with the wrong theory, the right instincts, and a notebook filling with the names of the dead.
Day 7 — The Survivor: the whole city, six weeks in — what London lost, what it kept, and why it is still here almost seven centuries later.


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🏰 ABOUT THIS SERIES
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
This is the complete "A Week in Medieval London (1348)" series from Time Warp Cities — a channel that reconstructs the daily texture of the past, one day, one life, and one city at a time. If you're fascinated by the Black Death, the bubonic plague, the Middle Ages, medieval England, and the real social history of how ordinary people lived, worked, and died, this full documentary is made for you.

We cover the history of the plague in London: how it spread along trade routes from Europe, why medieval medicine and miasma theory failed against it, what the East Smithfield mass burials reveal to archaeologists today, how the labour shortage that followed cracked the foundations of feudalism, and how the city survived and rebuilt — through 1348, the later plague returns, the Great Fire of 1666, and beyond.

Which of the seven days stayed with you the longest — the apprentice, the monk, the silk woman, the gravedigger, the alderman, the physician, or the survivor? Tell us in the comments.

snippet.title: The Terrifying 17th Century War That Wiped Out Millions
snippet.description:
The 30 Years War fractured Europe and rewrote the rules of power through blood and betrayal. What began as a fierce religious conflict between Catholics and Protestants quickly mutated into a continent-wide struggle for absolute dominance. This historical documentary exposes the hidden realities of the conflict through the eyes of those who lived it. Witness the dangerous double life of the legendary painter Peter Paul Rubens as he traded art for international espionage. See how a beggar monk named Father Joseph built a terrifyingly vast network of global informants to control the French throne from the shadows. From the gritty, survival-driven daily diary entries of Peter Hagendorf, a mercenary fighting for the highest bidder, to the megalomaniacal engineering marvel of a massive sea dam built to crush the rebellion at La Rochelle, this episode lays bare the tactical genius and horrific human cost of the world's first modern war.

snippet.title: Paris - 1600s
snippet.description:
Step into the grandeur of 17th-century Paris with an AI-generated reconstruction, inspired by the meticulous engravings, painted cityscapes, and architectural plans created throughout the early reign of Louis XIV. This visualisation draws heavily from the works of Jacques Callot, Israel Silvestre, and other court-appointed artists whose observational drawings captured Paris as it transformed into the political and cultural heart of France. All historical details are interpreted using AI for cinematic presentation, but great care has been taken to remain faithful to the colours, materials, and spatial character of Paris as it appeared at the time.

During this century, Paris was undergoing extraordinary change. Streets were widened, new bridges and quays were built along the Seine, and monumental projects began to reflect the growing power of the Bourbon monarchy. By mid-century, under the guidance of Louis XIV and his ministers, the city shifted from its medieval fabric toward a more ordered, classical vision — a process that would accelerate after 1661 when Louis took direct control of the state.

Artists like Silvestre documented this evolving metropolis in lavish detail: the Louvre still partly medieval but expanding toward its classical façades; the Île de la Cité alive with markets and churches; the Marais rising as the district of nobles; and the newly completed Place Royale (now Place des Vosges) standing as an early symbol of royal urban planning.

One of the most influential visual records from this era is Israel Silvestre’s panoramic Paris engravings, produced during his tenure as Louis XIV’s official court draughtsman. Although not always perfectly measured — perspectives were sometimes adjusted, alignments idealised, and architectural details refined to emphasize harmony — these works remain unmatched as windows into the pre-Haussmann, pre-Revolutionary city.

This reconstruction seeks to echo that spirit: historically grounded, artistically interpreted, and dedicated to showing Paris just as it stood on the threshold of becoming the great capital of Louis XIV’s France.

snippet.title: Life 900 Years Ago | How the Khmer Built Angkor Wat
snippet.description:
900 years ago, in the heart of the Khmer Empire, humans achieved the impossible — they built Angkor Wat, one of the largest religious monuments in the world.
This cinematic journey takes you back to the 12th century, when life was harsh, work was grueling, and yet, through sheer determination, skill, and unity, the Khmer people raised a temple that still stands as a testament to human ingenuity.

Follow the workers, artisans, and King Suryavarman II’s vision in a story that reveals:

How massive sandstone blocks were quarried, transported, and lifted without modern machines

The ingenious ramps, pulleys, sledges, and teamwork that made construction possible

The sweat, sacrifice, daily life, and celebrations of the workers and villagers who brought Angkor Wat to life

The carvings, towers, and final completion that immortalized a civilization in stone

More than stone, this is a story of human willpower, innovation, and culture in the 12th century — a monument raised by hand, devotion, and collective effort that still defies time.

snippet.title: Experience a Week in Ancient Egypt | Day 3: The Egyptian Priest
snippet.description:
Every morning, before the sun rises, a man enters a room smaller than a closet. He is alone. He unlocks a golden cabinet. And he dresses a god.

This is Day 3 of our 7-part series: Experience a Week in Ancient Egypt.

Today, you are a priest at Karnak Temple — the largest religious complex ever built. Before dawn you shave every hair from your body, bathe three times in a sacred lake, and dress in linen so fine you can see through it. Then you walk into the inner sanctuary and perform a ritual that, if done incorrectly, the priests believe will cause the sun not to rise tomorrow.

This is not metaphor. To the Egyptian mind, this is operational reality.

You will sing a twenty-minute hymn to a two-foot solid gold statue. You will feed him bread, beer, and roasted goose. You will back out of the room sweeping your own footprints from the floor so as not to leave a trace in the divine presence. And then you will spend the rest of your day running one of the most powerful institutions in the ancient world — a temple that owns fifteen percent of all farmland in Egypt, its own ships, its own granaries, and its own schools.

Using AI trained on archaeological evidence, surviving temple records, and the actual hymns carved into Karnak's walls, we've reconstructed what one day as an Egyptian priest actually looked like.

📅 SERIES SCHEDULE:
Day 1 — The Farmer
Day 2 — The Tomb Builder
Day 3 — The Egyptian Priest (you are here)
Day 4 — The Egyptian Wife
Day 5 — The Soldier
Day 6 — The Physician
Day 7 — The Festival of Opet (series finale)

🔔 Subscribe so you don't miss Day 4 — an Egyptian wife who runs a business, keeps the books, and has more legal rights than European women will have for another 3,000 years.

snippet.title: The Entire History of Ancient Mesopotamia — The Civilization That Built the World
snippet.description:
Before Rome. Before Greece. Before Egypt raised a single pyramid.

There was a civilisation between two rivers that gave the world almost everything it would later take credit for.

The wheel.
Writing.
Mathematics.
The sixty-minute hour.
The first law code.
The first love poem.
The first recipe.
The first map of the world.

They built the first cities in human history — cities with schools, courts, hospitals, and tax collectors.

They looked up at the night sky, named every star they could see, and calculated the movements of planets with an accuracy that would not be matched for another two thousand years.

They wrote down their fears, their prayers, their business transactions, and their epic poems — on clay tablets that are still being read today.

And then — empire by empire, century by century — they collapsed. Conquered, forgotten, buried under the desert sand.

Their name has almost vanished from history.

Their legacy has not.

Every time you check the time, divide a circle into three hundred and sixty degrees, or read a story about a great flood — you are living inside a world the people of Mesopotamia built.

This is their story.

snippet.title: What Kyoto ACTUALLY Looked Like After It Burned (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
Basically, in this video, I use AI to "resurrect" Kyoto—located in medieval Japan—exactly as it was in 1461, right before and during its catastrophic decade of destruction. It's not just about looking at temples; we explore the city at its most broken: a capital where 82,000 corpses dammed the Kamo River, while the shogun inside his palace hosted poetry competitions. We contrast that violent, chaotic reality with the stunning cultural legacy that emerged from those same ashes.

We also break down the exact political collapse that triggered the Onin War—how a succession dispute between two warlords sent a quarter million soldiers into a city built of wood, paper, and straw—and how the commoners who survived invented Japan's first form of civil self-government. It's crazy to see how everything the world calls "Japanese culture" — the tea ceremony, zen gardens, wabi-sabi, kintsugi — was born directly from a city that lost 80% of everything it had ever built.

snippet.title: Experience a Week in the Stone Age | Day 4: Surviving the Wilderness 12,000 Years Ago | The Traveler
snippet.description:
Three young men leave camp before dawn and walk north into country none of them has ever seen. They carry dried fish, water skins, and spare bowstrings — but the only thing that can keep them alive isn't in their packs. It's a map made entirely of memory, poured into their heads by an old man who could no longer make the journey himself.
Welcome to Day 4 of A Week in the Stone Age — a 7-part series following ordinary people through daily life 12,000 years ago, on the shores of a lake in what is now Yorkshire, England.
The camp is almost out of flint — and without it, there are no blades, no arrow points, no hunting. The only source is three days north, across rivers that drown the careless and marshes that swallow the unwary. And when the travellers finally reach it, they find they are not alone: another band already lives beside the stone. What happens next isn't a fight. It's something far older, and far more human.
In this episode:
→ The "oral map" that guided three men across country they'd never seen — with no writing, no paper, no marks of any kind
→ How to read a river that can kill you — and why the safe crossing looks worse than the deadly one
→ The flint source that could save a 40-person band
→ What really happened when two Stone Age tribes met over a scarce resource
→ The open hand — a peace protocol older than any language
→ Why the elder was never the one being carried
📍 Based on real archaeological evidence from Star Carr, Yorkshire — the most important Mesolithic site in Britain (c. 9,300–8,480 BC)

snippet.title: Roman London Revealed (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
Step back in time over 2,000 years to discover Roman London, a city lost beneath the streets of the modern capital. In this immersive documentary, we explore Londinium as it once was — its bustling streets, monumental buildings, thriving marketplaces, and the daily lives of its people.

With the power of AI reconstruction, experience the grandeur of the Roman Forum, the mystery of the London Mithraeum, and the drama of the amphitheatre as if you were walking its streets yourself. Witness how Roman engineers, merchants, and citizens shaped the foundations of what would one day become modern London.

Discover:

How Londinium rose from a military outpost to a thriving provincial capital.

The lives of women, traders, and craftsmen in Roman society.

The city’s economy, trade networks, and public entertainment.

Key events, including Boudica’s revolt and the city’s rebuilding.

🔹 Journey beneath the surface of London and uncover the hidden history that still shapes the city today.

Watch now and step into the lost world of Roman London.

snippet.title: Anne Askew’s Final Days Were Worst Than Death
snippet.description: Join us as we pull back the heavy curtain on the brutal reality of Tudor politics and expose the horrifying, historically accurate final days of Anne Askew. While history books often gloss over the sheer cruelty of the English Reformation, the true story of this 25-year-old poet and Protestant martyr is one of the most agonizing tales of state-sanctioned terror ever recorded. In this video, we trace her harrowing journey in July 1546 from her illegal imprisonment in the Tower of London to her public execution at Smithfield. We dive deep into the forensic and administrative records of her interrogation, revealing how she became the only woman to ever be officially tortured on the infamous Rack—turned so violently by the Lord Chancellor himself that her shoulders, hips, knees, and elbows were completely dislocated. Discover how her executioners had to carry her to the stake in a chair because she could no longer stand, and why the English crown's desperate attempt to break her spirit ultimately backfired, transforming a broken body into an immortal symbol of defiance. Hit play to uncover the devastating truth behind the legend.
